content: 1. Decision-makers have been sensitized to the importance of leprosy control and elimination efforts. Partnerships with organizations such as WHO, NGOs, and philanthropists are being sustained, as necessary, to ensure the continuation of essential leprosy services. These partnerships have been established with adequate funding allocated for related activities. 2. Flexible administrative models for treatment are being implemented to ensure the completion of therapy for migrants and refugees. Data on new autochthonous (locally transmitted) and non-autochthonous cases, treatment completion rates, and relapses are being monitored. 3. Trained personnel and adequate infrastructure at referral levels are essential for managing leprosy-related reactions and disabilities. Skilled healthcare workers are available at these levels to provide necessary care. 4. Effective surveillance systems and improved data management are being prioritized. This includes the digitization of data, the availability of web-based data management systems, and the mapping of new leprosy cases across all age groups at sub-national levels. Case-based data management systems are being linked with surveillance systems to track any new cases. 5. Contact tracing involves listing and mapping the contacts of all new cases, providing counseling, and ensuring comprehensive contact screening coverage. 6. Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) is being administered to eligible contacts of non-autochthonous cases through screening. Preventive chemotherapy is being provided to the maximum number of eligible contacts. 7. Proper documentation and investigation of all new cases, whether clustered or sporadic, are being conducted at sub-national levels and included in country dossiers. 8. Leprosy Transmission Assessment Surveys (LTAS) are not applicable in certain contexts but remain a tool for monitoring transmission trends. 9. Monitoring, evaluation, and verification systems are in place to ascertain cut-off levels for leprosy elimination. Internal monitoring by health services, web-based reporting systems to alert new cases, mandatory notification of leprosy, and surveillance systems to detect sporadic cases are being utilized. 10. Research is being conducted to develop innovative approaches to reach refugees, migrants, and displaced populations with leprosy services. 11. Data from sub-national levels in countries like Brazil and India have been analyzed to review trends in reaching cut-off levels for leprosy elimination. For example, Brazil, one of the top three endemic countries, reported an average of 28,000 new cases annually in recent years. Analysis of data from 20 municipalities showed a significant reduction in new cases, particularly among children and young adults, indicating a decrease in transmission. 12. In Tamil Nadu, India, data from two low-endemic districts (Chennai and Thoothukudi) were analyzed. While new cases have declined, sporadic cases continue to occur, highlighting the need for active case detection in endemic areas. 13. In low-burden countries like the Maldives and Morocco, data over the last 20 years were analyzed to assess progress toward elimination. The Maldives achieved significant reductions in leprosy prevalence, with many islands reaching benchmarks for elimination. However, sporadic cases in some areas, such as the capital Male’, reversed local elimination status temporarily. 14. Morocco has made progress in achieving interruption of transmission in most regions, but some provinces are yet to achieve this status. Sporadic cases during post-elimination surveillance periods have raised questions about the sufficiency of the ten-year follow-up period. 15. In Thailand and Vietnam, similar analyses have been conducted to track progress toward interruption of transmission and disease elimination. Maps indicate the movement of provinces toward these goals over the years, with some areas achieving post-elimination surveillance completion. 16. The importance of thorough investigation of every detected case during post-elimination surveillance is emphasized to maintain elimination status. Rare cases detected after ten years of follow-up highlight the need for integrated surveillance systems to ensure continued detection and management of leprosy cases.
